## The IDE workspace and the webR workspace {#what-we-use-today .smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.small}
**The IDE workspace**

- The folder that you downloaded, opened in Positron, RStudio, VS Code or another IDE
- Quarto renders your report; `fixest` fits your models
- No git, no cloning, no configuration – it is just files
- This is what I drive on the shared screen
:::
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.small}
**The webR workspace**

- One web page. R is compiled to run **inside the browser**
- Nothing installed, nothing to break, data already in place
- The same tasks, data and helpers, on the shared screen and in your own tab
- Your spare if your installation misbehaves at any point
:::
:::
::::

::: {.urlbox .fragment}
[github.com/CodeMoreh/ar4ds-eu-workspace](https://github.com/CodeMoreh/ar4ds-eu-workspace) [– download zip → unzip → open in your IDE]{.fs-80}
:::

::: notes
The IDE workspace is the folder that you downloaded, opened in your IDE, which is Positron on my screen and may be RStudio or VS Code on yours. Quarto renders your report and fixest fits your models, and there is no git and no cloning, because the workspace is only a folder of files. I drive it on the shared screen, so that you can follow keystroke for keystroke. The webR workspace is one web page, with R compiled to run inside the browser, nothing to install and the data already in place. Every task exists in both, with the same data and the same helper functions, so you can switch at any point if your machine misbehaves. [advance] The address of the IDE workspace is at the bottom of the slide, and it is also on the setup page.
:::

## What the tools cannot do {.smaller}

:::: {.none}
::: {.fragment}
A perfectly reproducible pipeline can be a perfectly reproducible answer to **a question you never stated**.
:::

::: {.fragment}
None of this software will tell you what your estimand is, whether your controls belong in the model, or whether the association you found means what you think it means.
:::

::: {.fragment}
Tooling is the **cheap** half of the problem, because it can be learned. **The expensive half is the question that the analysis is meant to answer.**
:::
::::

::: notes
All of this software is worth having. [advance] Yet a perfectly reproducible pipeline can be a perfectly reproducible answer to a question that you never stated, [advance] and no software will tell you what your estimand is, whether the variables that you put in the model belong there, or whether the association that you found means what you think it means. [advance] Tooling is the cheap half of the problem, in the sense that it can be learned, while the expensive half starts from a question that every quantitative study has to answer, namely what exactly you are trying to estimate, and much of what follows is about that question. First, though, you need a setup that works.
:::
